note: Gum-resin ('tear') of an Arabian tree; bdellium usually equated with guggul (C. wightii) or African bdellium; source species debated.
Frankincense from Arabia 'libanotophoros': Boswellia sacra; Indian libanos possibly B. serrata.
Pitys and the related peuke (pines); pitys usually Aleppo pine, peuke black pine; strobilos = stone pine. Genus Pinus certain.
Astringent shrub whose resin (schinine, mastiche) is best from Chios: mastic tree (standard).
Terebinth tree with edible fruit and resin; standard identification.
Liquid and dry pitch drawn from the resinous wood of peuke and pitys (pines).
Natural bitumen; Judaean (Dead Sea) best, also Phoenicia, Sidon, Babylon.
Standard identification; leaves and green cones ('sphairia') used.
Large and small arkeuthos; berries hazelnut- to bean-sized. Prickly juniper usual; large kind possibly J. drupacea.
Cypress-like, heavy-smelling, low spreading; abortifacient: savin (standard). Second, tamarisk-leaved kind uncertain.
Large tree yielding kedria (cedar pitch, embalming); small spiny kedros with juniper-like berries is a Juniperus.
Narrow- and broad-leaved daphne are both bay laurel; standard identification.
Plane tree native to Greece; standard identification.
Melia is ash; Greek species most likely manna ash or narrow-leaved ash.
Leuke = white poplar, paired with aigeiros (black poplar); standard.
Thick yellowish astringent bark from 'barbarian' lands, for dysentery; identity uncertain (kurchi bark proposed; medieval confusion with mace).
Aigeiros = black poplar; resin and Eridanus amber legend mentioned.
Ptelea = elm; field elm the common Mediterranean species.
Several reeds listed; medicinal root is of phragmites (common reed); donax/Cyprian reed = giant cane.
Plant from which paper (chartes) is made; standard.
Wild tamarisk by lakes; cultivated Egyptian/Syrian kind with gall-like 'fruit' probably T. aphylla. Species not determinable.
Bushy tamarisk-like shrub visited by bees for poor honey; heath (tree heath standard).
Seed of an Egyptian shrub used in eye-salves; Fraas/Berendes proposed Cassia absus (chaksu seed), speculative.
Thorny hedge shrub with oblong soft fleshy leaves, three kinds; Lycium europaeum or Rhamnus spp. proposed.
Spineless coastal hedge shrub with olive-like broader leaves, eaten boiled: Atriplex halimus (standard).
Well-known spiny shrub with oily seed; standard identification.
Pear-like very spiny small tree, red myrtle-sized fruit with stones: hawthorn; synonym pyrakantha suggests firethorn for some.
Tree-like thorny shrub, white flower, oblong red fruit woolly inside: wild rose (dog rose standard).
Olive-like leaves, white fragrant clustered flowers, best from Ascalon and Canopus: henna (standard).
Olive-like broader darker leaves, black sweetish clustered fruit; not lime-tree: Phillyrea (Berendes).
Male purple-flowered and female white-flowered cistus; also hypocistis (Cytinus) and ledon yielding ladanum.
Best ebony Ethiopian (African blackwood); Indian kind with streaks is Diospyros ebony.
Rose petals for juice and pastilles; ancient garden rose usually read as R. gallica/damascena group.
Extract of a thorny box-leaved shrub from Cappadocia/Lycia (Rhamnus spp.); Indian lycium from Berberis.
Juice from pods of an Egyptian thorny tree with white flowers and lupin-like pods: Acacia (Vachellia) nilotica.
Watery dregs of pressed olives boiled down.
Agnos or lygos: riverside shrub, olive-like leaves, purple/white flowers; standard.
Itea = willow; species not specified, white willow usual reading.
Wild olive (kotinos, var. sylvestris), with olive oils and 'Ethiopian olive' tear.
All oaks (drys, phegos, prinos); Sardian acorns (kastaneia) are chestnuts.
Oak galls; best omphakitis (small, knobby, unperforated) = Aleppo galls of Q. infectoria.
Culinary rhous from the tanners' sumac shrub, serrate leaves, clustered fruit; standard.
Egyptian dates (phoinikobalanoi, karyotides); standard.
Pomegranate fruit, rind (sidia), flowers (kytinoi), roots; standard.
Flower of wild pomegranate; standard.
Cultivated myrtle, black and white kinds; standard.
Cherries and cherry-tree gum; sweet or sour cherry not distinguished.
Carob pods; standard.
Apple trees generally, especially quince; also Persian (peach), Armenian (apricot) and Median apples (citron).
Many kinds of pear; achras = wild pear (P. spinosa).
Large 'lotus tree', sweet fruit bigger than pepper, wood yellows hair: Celtis australis (Berendes); Ziziphus lotus alternative.
Thorny aronia with small three-stoned apple-like fruit = azarole; Italian second kind (setanion) = medlar.
Olive-like oblong fruit turning yellow/waxy, edible, astringent; standard.
Oua (sorbs) dried for diarrhoea; standard.
Plum tree; Damascene dried plums; wild plums also mentioned.
Thin-barked tree with stoneless 'memaikyla' fruit; standard.
Bitter and sweet almonds; standard.
Syrian pistachios; standard.
Royal or Persian nuts = walnut; standard.
Morea or sykaminon: mulberry (black mulberry in antiquity); standard.
Large fig-like tree with mulberry-like leaves, fruit scraped to ripen; standard.
Fresh and dried figs, wild-fig sap, fig-wood lye; standard.
Egyptian tree with edible fruit, esp. Thebaid: Egyptian persea (Mimusops), not avocado; poison legend.
Pond plant with hat-like leaf, rose flower, wasp-nest seed head (kiborion), root kolokasion; standard.
Lentil; standard.
Narrow-leaved small plant with podded seed yielding orobinon flour; standard.
Cultivated lupin; smaller wild lupin also mentioned.
Turnip root, sprouts, seed; a wild gongyle is also described.
Bounias, a turnip-like root vegetable: navew (Brassica napus) per standard glossaries.
Garden radish; wild radish (horseradish per some) also treated.
Known root vegetable eaten boiled; skirret per standard glossaries, parsnip alternative.
Four kinds: marsh oxylapathon, garden, small wild, and oxalis (sorrel); all docks.
'Horse-dock': a large dock of marshes; species uncertain.
Wild pot-herb more nourishing than dock; glossed charlock (LSJ), Linnaeus' Lapsana borrowed the name.
Bland pot-herb without drug action; blite (Amaranthus blitum) standard.
Garden and wild mallow; common mallow usual reading.
Wild and garden orache eaten boiled; standard.
Cultivated cabbage; standard.
Coastal cliff cabbage, whiter, hairier, bitter: Aegean wild Brassica (B. cretica) or wild B. oleracea.
Kidney-shaped leaves on reddish ivy-like shoots, milky salty sap, strongly purgative: sea bindweed (standard).
Black and white beet; standard.
Cooling astringent pot-herb; standard.
Rock or prickly asparagus (myakanthos): spiny wild Mediterranean asparagus.
Two kinds: greater plantain and small narrow-leaved (ribwort); standard.
Aquatic umbellifer with hipposelinon-like aromatic leaves; Sium angustifolium (Berula) per Berendes.
Aquatic herb tasting like kardamon, called kardamine: watercress (standard).
Seashore rock plant with fleshy salty leaves, pickled; standard.
Prostrate herb with cut leaves, eaten boiled: buck's-horn plantain usual reading.
Two kinds: spinier (S. asper) and tender edible (S. oleraceus); standard.
Wild seris (pikris) and two garden kinds: endive and chicory group.
Chicory-like slender plant with mastic-like gum on stems; second kind unidentified.
Edible kolokynthe of antiquity is the bottle gourd (Cucurbita is American).
Janick & Paris 2007: classical sikys mostly snake/chate melon (traditionally cucumber); pepon (melon) also treated.
Garden lettuce; wild lettuce with opium-like latex also treated.
Wild-carrot-like bitter Syrian/Cilician pot-herb; equated with Daucus gingidium/Ammi visnaga; uncertain.
Wild bitter pot-herb eaten raw or boiled; standard.
Span-high hairy umbellifer, fennel-like leaves, white fragrant umbel, eaten; modern Greek kafkalithra = Tordylium apulum; uncertain.
Aphrodisiac salad herb and seed; standard.
Basil; standard.
Leafless reddish parasitic stem choking pulses, eaten like asparagus: broomrape (O. crenata on legumes).
